title: Mamluk Sultanate
capsule: The Mamluk Sultanate of Cairo (1250–1517) was founded when Mamluk officers of the Ayyubid army deposed the last Ayyubid sultan of Egypt and established their own military monarchy. Sultan Baybars I (r. 1260–1277) defined the sultanate's strategic character by defeating the Mongols at 'Ayn Jalut in 1260 — the first major Mongol battlefield defeat — and systematically dismantling the remaining Crusader states in Syria and Palestine. The Bahri (Turkic) period gave way to the Burji (Circassian) phase after 1382, during which sultans including Barquq and Qaitbay maintained Egypt as the wealthiest state in the medieval Islamic world, controlling the Red Sea spice trade. The Ottoman sultan Selim I crushed the Mamluk forces at the Battle of Marj Dabiq in 1516 and at Raydaniyya in 1517, incorporating Egypt and the Levant into the Ottoman Empire.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Core territories in Egypt, Syria, and the Hejaz are well documented through Arabic chronicles, administrative registers (diwans), and diplomatic correspondence; frontier zones in Anatolia and Nubia are less precisely bounded.
